title: The Too-Pretty Invitations
markdown:
The evening air was growing soft and mellow, like warm honey drizzled over the day, and the world was beginning to hum a quiet sleepy tune. Down by the whispering reeds, where the water lapped gently against the shore, Lottie the duck gave a little happy sigh, a sound like a soft feather rustling. She was nestled beside her very best friend, Otis the otter, and they were watching the first shy stars begin to wink in the dimming sky, like tiny diamonds sprinkled on a dark blue blanket.

“It’s almost time for Uncle Pipkin’s Moon-Viewing Supper,” Lottie chirped, a happy little wiggle making her feathers fluff. “He always makes the most yummy dandelion tea, the kind that warms you right down to your toes, and the moon looks like a giant pearly button when it peeks over the sleepy hills. And he tells the most wonderful stories.”

Otis, sleek and calm, with eyes like smooth pebbles, nudged Lottie gently with his nose. “And he tells the best stories,” he whispered, his voice like the gentle flow of a stream over smooth stones. “Stories that feel like warm blankets. I can almost feel the moonlight already, can’t you?”

This supper was a very special occasion, a time for all their woodland friends to gather and marvel at the moon. Usually the invitations arrived in the mail a few days before, delivered by the ever-so-neat Mr. Quill, the letter keeper.

Mr. Quill was a hedgehog of immense neatness. His spines were always brushed to a perfect shine, his waistcoat always buttoned in a straight line, and his parcels always tied with the most perfectly symmetrical bows you ever did see. He also loved to make things beautiful. It was a secret joy. He saw beauty in the dewdrop on a leaf, in the pattern of a spider’s web, and especially in making the everyday things of life look lovely.

This year, Mr. Quill decided, the invitations to Uncle Pipkin’s Moon-Viewing Supper would be extra special. He had a whole stack of thick creamy paper that felt like soft petals, and a box of the brightest most wonderful paints he had ever seen. “These invitations,” he murmured, his tiny nose twitching with delight, “will be so lovely, so captivating, that everyone will simply have to open them to see what wonderful secrets they hold.”

And so he began to paint. For the first invitation he painted a shimmering silver moon, so real you almost felt you could reach out and touch its soft glow. For the next he drew a whole family of sleepy owls, their big round eyes like golden coins, nestled in a cozy branch. Then came a delicate swirl of stardust that seemed to shimmer with captured moonlight, and a row of twinkling fireflies, each one a tiny glowing jewel painted with painstaking care. Each envelope was a tiny work of art. Mr. Quill was so pleased that he hummed a little tune as he finished the very last one, tying it with a silken ribbon the colour of twilight.

Too pretty to open. Too lovely to unfold.

The next day, Lottie and Otis were so excited to check their mailboxes. “Oh, I truly hoped there would be one,” Lottie quacked, waddling hopefully towards her little blue box. Otis peered into his, his whiskers twitching, his smooth fur gleaming in the gentle morning light.

And there they were. Beautiful artistic invitations. Lottie’s had a painting of a laughing moonbeam, all swirls of silver and light. Otis’s had a delicate drawing of a sleepy blossom, its petals unfurling in the softest hues of pink and white. They were too pretty to open. They were too lovely to disturb.

“Oh, Lottie,” Otis murmured, his voice hushed with wonder, “it’s too lovely to unfold. It feels like a shame to smooth out all those lovely swirls and pictures. It’s like a tiny piece of the night sky, all caught in my paws.”

Lottie nodded, tilting her head. “It is rather like a little painting, isn’t it? I wouldn’t want to smush the moonbeam. It looks so happy just as it is.”

They carefully placed their beautiful invitations on a sunny patch of moss, where the dappled light made the artwork even more enchanting. They admired them, turning them this way and that. Then Lottie’s tummy did a little flip, like a tiny bird learning to fly. “But if we don’t open them,” she said softly, “how will we know what time the supper is? Or what yummy things Uncle Pipkin might want us to bring? He did mention something about Mrs. Higgins’s famous blueberry muffins.”

Soon other friends came by, chattering excitedly about the beautiful invitations they had received. Gruffudd Bear had one with a magnificent rainbow arcing across it, and Penelope Possum had one with a sky full of sleepy clouds shaped like fluffy sheep. But everywhere the same thing was happening. The invitations were admired, placed on shelves and windowsills, kept safe as precious treasures, but no one was opening them. A soft sigh grew from their gentle worry.

Uncle Pipkin himself came to check on his guests, his long ears twitching with gentle concern. He saw Lottie and Otis looking a little puzzled, their happy excitement dimmed. “It seems my friends have received invitations so beautiful, they are afraid to disturb their loveliness. They are like precious gems, not to be opened.”

Lottie and Otis looked at each other. “But Uncle Pipkin,” Lottie said, her voice small and earnest, “we need to know when to come. We don’t want to be late for the dandelion tea.”

Otis added, “And maybe there are instructions about yummy berry pies. Or Mrs. Higgins’s muffins.”

Uncle Pipkin chuckled, a warm rumbling sound that seemed to settle the worried breeze. “Sometimes, when things are very, very beautiful, their true purpose can be a little hidden, like a shy creature behind a leaf. Perhaps we should visit Mr. Quill. He means well, of course, but sometimes his passion for beauty can lead him a little astray.”

And so Lottie and Otis, with Uncle Pipkin hopping gently beside them, waddled and slid their way to the little post office. Mr. Quill was busy polishing his spectacles, his spines gleaming, looking very pleased with himself.

“Mr. Quill,” Lottie called out, trying to sound bright. “Your invitations are simply the most beautiful things we have ever seen. They are like tiny pieces of art.”

“Oh, thank you, thank you,” Mr. Quill puffed up, his chest swelling with pride. “I do try my best to make everything perfect. Look at this starry night. And this sleeping fox. Aren’t they lovely?” He beamed, showing them the intricate work on one of the envelopes.

Otis swam a little circle in a nearby puddle, then dried himself carefully with a shake. “They are indeed, Mr. Quill,” he said gently. “So lovely, in fact, that none of us have quite managed to open them yet. We are too afraid to spoil their perfect drawings.”

Mr. Quill blinked, his neat little face wrinkling in confusion. “Not opened them?” he stammered. His voice lost some of its proud hum. “But the supper is tomorrow evening. Surely you need to know the time? And the directions? Uncle Pipkin is expecting everyone.” He looked around his neat little office. “My lovely paintings. Have they hidden the important bits? Has my beauty made a muddle?”

A quiet fell over the little post office, a hush as soft as falling snow. Mr. Quill’s spines drooped a little. “Oh dear,” he whispered. “My art has made a muddle.”

But Lottie, ever cheerful, nudged his paw with her beak. “It’s not a muddle, Mr. Quill. It’s just very, very artistic. We all agree. But we do need to know when to come for the dandelion tea and the stories.”

Otis nodded. “Perhaps we could have invitations that are beautiful and easy to open. Like a little picture on the outside of a plain envelope, so we know it’s special, but then we can open it to find all the wonderful details inside.”

Mr. Quill’s ears perked up. He looked at Lottie and Otis, then at Uncle Pipkin, who gave a wise encouraging nod. “A wonderful idea,” Uncle Pipkin declared. “A little bit of beauty to draw them in, and a clear message inside to guide them.”

Mr. Quill’s face brightened. “Yes. Yes, that’s it.” He scampered over to a shelf and pulled out a fresh stack of plain sturdy envelopes. Then, with quick neat strokes, he drew a single delicate moon on each one, a soft silver crescent. Inside he wrote in his neatest most readable handwriting: You are invited to Uncle Pipkin’s Moon-Viewing Supper. Starts when the first star twinkles. Please bring a smile.

Too pretty to open? Not these. A moon on the outside, a welcome within.

Soon the new invitations were delivered, simple and welcoming, with a hint of moon-magic on the outside and a clear happy message waiting within. And this time everyone happily opened them.

The next evening, as the first shy star began to twinkle, Lottie and Otis and all their friends arrived at Uncle Pipkin’s burrow. The air was warm and sweet, smelling of clover and damp earth. Inside, cozy lanterns cast a gentle dancing glow, and Uncle Pipkin was pouring delicious dandelion tea. The moon, a huge silvery disc, peeked over the hill, bathing the scene in its soft serene light.

Lottie and Otis sat together, snuggled close, sipping their tea. Gruffudd Bear’s rainbow invitation sat opened on a mossy stool, and Penelope’s sleepy-cloud one too. The invitations had been perfect after all: a little bit of beauty, a little bit of clarity, and a whole lot of friendship. As the moon climbed higher into the velvety sky, a deep peaceful quiet settled over them, and they all began to feel very sleepy, tucked safely in the warm glow of friendship and moonlight.
characters: Lottie (moon-supper duck), Otis (pebble-eyed otter), Uncle Pipkin (dandelion-tea host)
